3 MINUTES
A cat in a
box, a foam of
spacetime, and a universe
made of bits.
Three of physics' strangest
ideas, in under three minutes.
We cannot discuss quantum
theology without confronting
Erwin Schrödinger's infamous
thought experiment:
Schrödinger's Cat.
Devised in nineteen
thirty-five to illustrate
the sheer absurdity of
the Copenhagen
interpretation, the setup
is brutally simple.
A cat is placed
in a steel box
with a radioactive atom,
a Geiger counter,
a vial of poison,
and a hammer.
If the atom decays,
the hammer drops,
the poison shatters,
and the cat dies.
Taken literally, the
Copenhagen reading says
that until the box
is opened, the atom
is in a superposition
of both decayed and undecayed.
Therefore, the cat would
be both dead and alive!
Schrödinger meant this
as a criticism,
not as a prediction.
Decoherence offers a partial
answer.
Whenever a quantum system
interacts with its wider
environment, whether by
colliding with a stray
photon or bumping into
a single gas molecule,
its fragile quantum
coherence leaks irreversibly
into the surroundings.
The ghostly superposition
becomes impossible to
detect, and the system
behaves like classical,
solid reality.
In this picture,
no conscious observer is
needed to make the
world look definite;
the environment does that
work automatically.
But decoherence does not
by itself explain why
we see one single
outcome, and physicists
still debate that.
The modern quest for
ultimate truth has driven
physicists to attempt the
holy grail of science:
unifying Einstein's General
Relativity with Quantum
Mechanics into a Theory
of Everything.
But when you zoom
into the Planck scale,
the fabric of spacetime
may stop being smooth.
It is thought to
dissolve into Quantum Foam,
a boiling sea where
space and time fluctuate
wildly, perhaps even
twisting into microscopic
wormholes in some
speculative models.
At that scale,
the classical concept of
time may break down.
What, then, is the
fundamental nature of the
cosmos revealed by quantum
physics?
Pioneering theoretical
physicist John Archibald
Wheeler coined the legendary
phrase: It from Bit.
He proposed that all
physical entities, matter,
radiation, forces, and
spacetime itself, are
ultimately derived from
information.
Some physicists suspect
that the bedrock of
reality is not solid
clay but quantum bits,
qubits, processing through
entanglement and
superposition.
It remains a speculative idea.
